transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me a little bit about what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it’s... it’s a very long story, but my husband insisted I come talk to someone, though honestly, I think he’s just tired of me pointing out the obvious. I’m here because for nearly two years now—twenty-two months, if you want to be exact, ever since we decided to update the house—I’ve been absolutely sure that our contractor and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together behind my back. 

It started with just small things, you know, a delay here, a missing tool there, but now it is clear as day that they are colluding to cheat us. They are keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. The cabinets don't align just right, the tile grout is completely the wrong shade of gray, the sink drips in this very deliberate way... and it's all intentional. It really is. They want to wear me down. 

My husband, bless his heart, he just doesn't see it. He keeps pulling out this thick manila folder and showing me all these receipts, pointing at the item numbers and the dates, trying to prove everything is perfectly normal. And that contractor, Gary, he always has a million excuses ready—oh, it's the supply chain, oh, the house foundation is settling, oh, the humidity is warping the wood. But I see the way the neighbors look at his truck when he pulls up, and I know they are all in on it together to ruin my home, no matter how many pieces of paper my husband waves in my face or how many lies they tell me.

Aside from what you've noticed about the contractor and your neighbors, have you been experiencing any unusual sensations, like hearing voices when no one is around or feeling like people are trying to communicate with you through hidden messages on the television or radio?

Voices? Oh, heavens, no. No, no, no. I mean, I know exactly why you’re asking me that—I’m sure my husband probably made it sound like I’m sitting around losing my marbles or something, but I am perfectly sound of mind. I don’t hear anyone talking when I’m alone in the house. Well, except for the neighbor's dog, but he just barks at the mailman like any normal dog would. 

And as for the television... no, that’s just silly. I watch the local news channel every morning with my cup of coffee—just regular Folgers, I've never been one for those expensive coffee shop drinks—and then in the evenings we usually just put on Jeopardy or Wheel of Fortune. The people on the screen are just reading their cue cards, they certainly aren't sending me any secret codes or anything ridiculous like that. I don’t even listen to the radio much anymore, honestly, not since they changed the local station that used to play the good music from the seventies. 

So, no, absolutely nothing like that. I’m a very practical person, Dr. Smith. I only pay attention to what is actually happening right in front of my own two eyes. I don't need to imagine voices to know what's going on, because they are doing it right out in the open! It’s not the television I’m worried about, it’s what’s happening right in my own kitchen and out on my street. You don't need hidden messages to see that the grout in the backsplash is completely wrong, you just need a working pair of eyes! I mean, if you just saw the way Gary smirked at me on Tuesday when he said the wrong cabinet doors were a "factory error," you would know exactly what I mean. He just stood there, holding his little clipboard...

Aside from your concerns regarding the contractor and your neighbors, have you ever felt that there were other people or groups of people actively plotting against you in different areas of your life?

Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. It’s really just this whole mess with the house. I mean, my life used to be so wonderfully quiet, Dr. Smith. Before we started this renovation, I spent my days tending to my garden—I have the most beautiful hydrangeas, they really thrive in the morning sun on the east side of the house—and volunteering at the library down the street on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. The people there, the other volunteers, the librarians, they are just lovely. Mrs. Higgins, she’s the head librarian, she even brought me a tin of homemade snickerdoodles last Christmas. So, no, nobody at the library is plotting against me. 

And my family? Well, my husband, as I said, he’s just blind to what’s happening, but he means well. My daughter, Sarah, she lives three states away in Ohio, and she calls me every Sunday evening right after dinner, like clockwork. We just talk about her kids, my grandchildren, you know, little Tommy is starting soccer and Emma is taking piano lessons. She certainly isn’t involved in any sort of conspiracy against me. 

It’s really just Gary and the people on my block. I don't go around thinking the whole world is out to get me, I really don't. I just know what I see in my own home. I mean, if you had seen the state of my kitchen before we started, it was outdated, sure, with those awful oak cabinets from the nineties, but it was functional! Now, it’s just a daily reminder that they are trying to break my spirit. But no, outside of my street and that contractor, everyone else is perfectly fine. I just wish I could go back to the way things were before Gary and his crew ever stepped foot on my property.
Aside from what you see in your home, have you ever felt any unusual physical sensations on your skin, such as a feeling of crawling, burning, or being touched when no one is there?

Oh, my stars, no. Nothing like that at all. Crawling skin? Burning? Good heavens, Dr. Smith, I’m not... I’m not imagining bugs under my skin or anything from a horror movie. My skin is perfectly fine. Well, I mean, it gets a little dry in the wintertime, especially around February when the heater has been running non-stop. I have to use this special Eucerin cream—the one with the dark blue cap, not the light blue one, because the light blue one just doesn't absorb right—and I put it on my elbows and my knees every night before bed, otherwise they get terribly ashy and rough. 

But feeling things touching me when no one is there? Absolutely not. I would certainly know if something was touching me, and I wouldn't just make it up. I’m a very grounded person. I mean, my mother, God rest her soul, she used to say I was the most practical of all her girls. My sister Margaret, now she was a bit flighty, always convinced she felt a draft or had a chill, but me? No. I only feel what’s actually there. 

Like the other day, I was out in the garden trying to prune back the rose bushes—the ones by the front walkway, they grow so fast if you don't keep after them—and a thorn caught me right on the forearm. Just a little scratch, but I felt it, plain as day. That’s a real sensation. That’s something you can see the mark from. But this... this invisible touching or crawling? No, Dr. Smith, that’s just nonsense. I really think my husband has given you the wrong impression of me. I am not sitting around having hallucinations or feeling phantom hands. I am just a woman who wants her kitchen finished the way it was promised, and who is tired of being lied to by a contractor who is clearly up to no good. If Gary would just put the right hinges on the pantry door—the soft-close ones we paid extra for, not those cheap metal things that slam—I wouldn't even be here having to answer questions about my skin!

Since this started with the renovations, have you found that you are still able to handle your usual responsibilities, like your volunteer work at the library, or has this situation made it difficult for you to keep up with your normal routine?

Oh, heavens, yes. I haven't let this whole mess stop me from living my life, Dr. Smith. I mean, it’s terribly stressful, of course it is, having your home torn apart and knowing the people doing it are actively trying to make you miserable, but I am not the sort of woman who just takes to her bed and gives up. Outside of dealing with this awful remodel, I am still keeping up with everything exactly the way I usually do. 

My volunteer work at the library is going just fine, like I mentioned before. And my church gatherings—well, I haven't missed a Sunday service at First Presbyterian in, oh, it must be fifteen years, except for that time I had the terrible flu back in 2018. We have our fellowship coffee hour right after the service in the basement, and I always bring my lemon pound cake. Pastor Thomas always says it’s his favorite, though I suspect he says that to all the ladies who bake, bless his heart. But I’m still there every Sunday, serving coffee and setting up the folding chairs. 

And then there’s my book club. We meet every third Wednesday of the month. Right now we’re reading one of those historical fiction novels—set in World War II, you know, they all seem to be set in World War II these days, with the dual timelines and the letters found in the attic—and it's actually my turn to host next month. I’m just praying Gary and his crew have the kitchen in some sort of usable state by then, because I simply cannot serve store-bought cookies to the girls. Margaret, one of the ladies in the club, she always notices if you cut corners. But yes, I haven't missed a single meeting, and I always read the chapters we're assigned. 

My regular household routines haven't slipped one bit, either. I still do the laundry on Mondays, strip all the beds, wash the linens in hot water—you really have to use hot water to get them properly clean, no matter what those new cold-water detergents claim—and I do all my dusting on Thursdays. I even keep up with all our family plans. Sarah and I talk every Sunday without fail, and my husband and I still do our Friday night dinners at the Olive Garden, just like we always have. 

So, you see, my routine is perfectly intact. I am managing my life just fine. It’s just this one particular situation with the house and that contractor that is completely out of hand. If Gary thinks he can disrupt my entire life just by installing the wrong drawer pulls and smirking at me, well, he has another thing coming, because I refuse to let him win.
Before your husband suggested you come see me today, have you ever spoken to a doctor or another professional specifically about your concerns regarding the contractor and the neighbors?

Oh, heavens, why would I do that? I mean... a doctor? For a contractor who refuses to do his job properly? No, no, I certainly haven't. I see my regular doctor, Dr. Evans, of course. He is over at the clinic on Maple Street, and I have been going to him for, oh, it has to be twenty years now, ever since Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Boca Raton. And Dr. Evans is just wonderful, he really is, he keeps a very close eye on my blood pressure. I take a little pill for that every morning right with my oatmeal. But I would never dream of bringing up Gary and the kitchen remodel with Dr. Evans! What on earth would a general practitioner do about a man who is deliberately installing the wrong grade of drywall just to spite me? 

And as for other professionals... well, I suppose you mean like a lawyer or the police or something of that nature? I haven't done that either. I mean, I did think about calling the Better Business Bureau at one point. I even had their phone number written down on a little yellow sticky note right next to the telephone in the hallway. But my husband, he just kept telling me to let it go, to just get the kitchen finished and be done with it. He absolutely hates making a fuss, my husband does. He is the sort of man who will eat a cold steak at a restaurant rather than send it back to the kitchen, bless his heart. So, no, I didn't call anyone. I just tried to handle it myself by keeping a close eye on Gary's crew when they were working. 

So when my husband said I should come talk to you, a psychiatrist, of all things... well, I was just flabbergasted. I told him flat out that I do not need a doctor, I need a new contractor! But he was so terribly insistent, and he has been so stressed with the house being in such a state of disarray, that I finally just agreed to come today just to keep the peace in our marriage. But no, to answer your question, I haven't spoken to anyone else about this because it is simply not a medical problem, Dr. Smith. It is a construction problem.
